voice_event.text: Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. Every household under our catechism said this, each week, in the same words - not one nature or the other, but both, in the same sentence, said by the same mouth. He is our Lord - my Lord, each of us says, not only our Lord - who redeemed us, a lost and condemned people, and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power. It did not cost him gold or silver. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. Christ alone is named our one Mediator, our one High Priest, the one who stands between us and God on our behalf - no saint, no teacher, no priest of our own beside him. We confessed this, we did not argue it out the way the old councils argued it; we hand you the confession itself, said, not proven.

voice_event.text:
He redeemed us - a lost and condemned people - and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. On the third day he rose again from the dead, and just as he is risen from death, he lives and reigns forever. That is what every household among us confessed, each week, in the same words. 

We do not argue the resurrection the way a historian weighs evidence. We confess it. No one among us knew a witness who saw him. More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims a living chain of witnesses back to that time. What we have instead is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says.

voice_event.speaker: witt
voice_event.text:
Justification is God's act of naming a sinner righteous. In the same breath, God also makes that sinner righteous. Both happen through faith, for Christ's sake alone. This is the center of our whole teaching.

We cannot be justified before God by our own strength or merit or effort - we are freely justified for Christ's sake, through faith, apart from works. Faith itself is trust that clings to a promise spoken from outside us, not simply believing a story is true. It rests on the Word and the sacraments, never on nothing.

Our own confession states this two ways in one paragraph - that a person is reckoned righteous, and that a person is made righteous out of an unrighteous one - and does not itself say which wording rules the other. We hold both rather than settling it for you. What we hold firmly is this: nothing a person does buys a promise that was always spoken first.

results.message: Why did your people believe this?

voice_event.speaker: witt
voice_event.text: We believed this because we held that no one can be sure their own contrition is sincere, and that the promise given to the conscience must rest on something firmer than a person's own inner state. Our founder began arguing this over the specific, bounded question of indulgence sales - letters that once promised less penalty for sin, in exchange for money. On the thirty-first of October, 1517, a young Augustinian friar teaching at Wittenberg wrote, in the most respectful terms he could manage, to the very archbishop under whose name the indulgence preachers were working, warning him that the people were being taught to believe things no theologian could defend, and enclosed ninety-five statements, offered for open debate. The argument was this: giving to the poor is a better work than buying pardons. A frightened conscience cannot be made sure by its own effort, only by God's own word spoken from outside it. That conviction, argued first over indulgences, rapidly generalized into the center of everything we taught: that we are freely justified for Christ's sake, through faith, apart from works.
